meta.title: The potential adverse effects of hypodermic glucagon-like peptide -1 receptor agonist on patients with type 2 diabetes: A population-based study.
meta.abstract:
Background

Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs), a class of injectable antidiabetic drugs, have shown significant efficacies in improving glycemic and weight control in patients with type 2 diabetes (T2D). However, the long-term safety of GLP-1 RAs remains insufficiently studied. This study aimed to provide real-world evidence on potential adverse outcomes associated with GLP-1 RAs use in T2D patients without major chronic diseases including impaired cardiac or renal function.

Methods

We conducted a retrospective cohort study involving 7746 T2D patients on GLP-1 RAs in Shenzhen, China. They were compared with 124 371 metformin-only users and 36 146 insulin-only users, forming two therapy control groups. GLP-1 RAs users were also further 1:2 paired with the control groups. Competing risk survival analyses were conducted to assess the incidence risks, presenting subdistributional hazard ratios (sHRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for various adverse outcomes associated with GLP-1 RAs use.

Results

Compared with metformin-only users, GLP-1 RAs use was associated with increased risks of various adverse outcomes (sHRs with 95% CIs), including pancreatitis (2.01, 1.24-3.24), acute nephritis (3.20, 2.17-4.70), kidney failure (3.73, 2.74-5.08), thyroid cancer (2.25, 1.23-4.10), and thyroid dysfunction (1.27, 1.00-1.63), respectively; Similar results were also found when compared with insulin-only users. Importantly, long-term (≥12 months) GLP-1 RAs use may further elevate the incidence risks of pancreatitis, acute nephritis, thyroid cancer, and thyroid dysfunction.

Conclusion

Compared with traditional T2D treatments, GLP-1 RAs use may be associated with increased risks of various adverse outcomes in a Chinese population. Cautions were strongly warranted in the use of GLP-1 RAs. Further validation is crucial across diverse populations.

domains.name: Confounding
domains.direction_justification: GLP-1 RA users had higher baseline obesity (BMI 30.0-39.9: 13.21% vs 4.87% in metformin and 3.04% in insulin) and residual confounding persists because propensity score matching matched on 'Unspecified' categories for BMI (32.49% unspecified) and education (32.31% unspecified), while critical glycemic severity markers were not adjusted for due to massive missingness (HbA1c missing rate 90.52% to 91.79%), biasing risk estimates away from the null.

findings.title: Confounding by indication and disease severity
findings.mechanism: Patients prescribed GLP-1 RAs have different baseline cardiometabolic risk, duration of diabetes, and obesity profiles compared to metformin-only users, which directly predisposes them to pancreatitis and renal outcomes.
evidence: Baseline BMI 30.0-39.9 kg/m2 was 13.21% in GLP-1 RAs vs 4.87% in metformin-only and 3.04% in insulin-only groups.
Metformin and insulin monotherapy represent substantially different disease severity stages in clinical practice.

findings.title: Inadequate adjustment due to matching on missing indicator categories
findings.mechanism: Matching on 'Unspecified' status as a discrete category fails to balance the true underlying continuous confounders (BMI, education, marital status), leaving substantial residual confounding.
evidence: Table 1 shows 32.49% of GLP-1 RA users and 32.71% of metformin controls had 'Unspecified' BMI.
Table 1 shows 19.74% of GLP-1 RA users and 20.00% of metformin controls had 'Unspecified' age category.

findings.title: Baseline paradox: worse starting position, better outcome
findings.mechanism: differential detection bias from higher socioeconomic status and insurance access; channelling/indication bias toward GLP-1 RAs for patients with refractory diabetes or higher obesity; residual confounding from unmeasured diabetes duration and missing laboratory values
evidence: The GLP-1 RA cohort was markedly younger (age ≥70: 5.72% vs 8.93% in metformin and 10.34% in insulin) and had lower fasting glucose (7.27 vs 7.68 mmol/L), yet exhibited substantially elevated hazard of acute nephritis (sHR 3.20, 95% CI 2.17–4.70), kidney failure (sHR 3.73, 95% CI 2.74–5.08), and leukemia (sHR 15.09, 95% CI 4.65–48.98) compared to metformin.

findings.title: Multiple testing and subgroup analysis without multiplicity correction
findings.mechanism: Testing dozens of adverse outcomes across several duration cutoffs (<12 vs >=12 months) and individual agents increases the likelihood of spurious associations (e.g., leukemia sHR 15.09).
evidence: Figure 3 and Figure 2 present multiple end-organ endpoints across digestive, renal, thyroid, skin, and hematopoietic systems without multiplicity adjustment.
Leukemia with sHR 15.09 (95% CI: 4.65-48.98) based on very few events.

overall.summary: This retrospective observational cohort study evaluating GLP-1 RA adverse effects against metformin and insulin monotherapies has a high overall risk of bias. The study is limited by severe confounding by indication and residual confounding: key confounders had heavy missingness (HbA1c missing in >90% of patients; BMI missing in ~32-34%), and propensity score matching included missingness as an 'Unspecified' category rather than balancing the actual biological variables. Furthermore, differential surveillance bias and multiple testing across dozens of unadjudicated EHR outcomes likely inflated risk estimates away from the null.

time_related_biases.summary: The study defines exposure retrospectively across the entire follow-up period, creating post-baseline conditioning and immortal time bias. Furthermore, the absence of any lag period with a mean follow-up under two years attributes slow-latency malignancies (thyroid cancer and leukemia) detected within months of prescription to drug exposure, strongly inflating apparent adverse risks through detection bias.

unverified_numbers.label: Selection of participants into the study — Exclusion of over 360,000 patients due to missing prescription records and restrictive monotherapy definitions over follow-up selects a non-representative survivor cohort with differential monitoring.

Massive attrition during cohort selection Excluding a large proportion of patients due to missing prescription records (362,035 out of 985,278 outpatients) creates potential selection bias. — 362,035 out of 985,278 diabetes outpatients (36.7%) were excluded due to missing prescription data.
